brief.name: LineDart
brief.tagline: Palm-sized PID line follower that holds 1 m/s
brief.description: A small differential-drive robot that follows a black line on a white surface. A Pololu QTR-8RC 8-channel reflectance array sits at the front, 68 mm ahead of the axle and 2.5 mm above the floor. An Arduino Nano reads it about every 1 ms, works out where the line is (0–7000), and runs a PID loop that sends differential PWM through a TB6612FNG dual H-bridge to two 30:1 micro metal gearmotors with 32 mm wheels. A 3/4" ball caster under the front deck takes the third contact point. Power comes from a 2S 460 mAh LiPo under a velcro strap on the deck. All electronics sit on one carrier PCB on 15 mm standoffs above the battery. The firmware also handles button-triggered sensor calibration, start/stop, and low-battery cutoff.

functional: Follow a 19 mm black line (electrical tape) on a white matte surface, including 90° corners and curves down to 100 mm radius
Button-triggered calibration: the robot spins in place for 2 s and records each channel's min/max reflectance
GO button starts and stops the run; the status LED shows idle, calibrating, running and low-battery
If the line is lost for more than 300 ms, search toward the side it was last seen; stop after 2 s
Measure battery voltage on A7 and stop the motors below 6.6 V (3.3 V per cell)
Reflash over the Nano's USB without taking anything apart

performance.averageLineSpeed: ≥ 1.0 m/s on a standard 2 m oval course
performance.topSpeed: about 1.6 m/s (30:1 HP motors at 7.4 V, 32 mm wheels)
performance.runtime: ≥ 20 min of continuous running on 460 mAh

constraints: Fits a 100 x 84 mm footprint and stays under 60 mm tall
Off-the-shelf modules only, plus one 2-layer carrier PCB and one laser-cut plate
All fasteners are M2, M2.5 or M3
Works from a 2S LiPo (6.6–8.4 V); the TB6612 VM limit is 13.5 V
Centre of gravity between the axle (z=-25) and the caster (z=22), biased toward the axle

brief.firmwarePlatform: Arduino (ATmega328P, Arduino Nano) via PlatformIO, using the Pololu QTRSensors library
risks: Running the 6 V HP motors at 8.4 V shortens brush life and pushes stall current to about 2 A, above the TB6612's 1.2 A continuous rating. Limit PWM duty to 75% in firmware and soft-ramp it.
2.5 mm sensor clearance can scrape on track seams or bumps; a nylon skid or a slight caster height increase may be needed
Ambient IR (sunlight or halogen light) can saturate the QTR-8RC; calibrate on site and consider a light shield
Battery strap slots and motor-wire holes weaken the 3 mm acrylic plate; use FR4 if it cracks
Motor brush noise can reset the Nano. Mitigate with 0.1 µF caps at the motors, 100 µF on VM, and separate ground returns.
Lack of encoders means no closed-loop speed control; speed drifts as battery voltage sags, so scale PWM to battery voltage
The front-mounted 75 mm sensor board is exposed to collision damage

electronics.summary: LineDart carrier PCB: a 2S LiPo (6.6–8.4 V) connects at J1 (JST-PH) and runs through a 3 A fast fuse (F1), a P-MOSFET for reverse-polarity protection (Q1) and a second P-MOSFET high-side switch (Q2). Q2 is turned on by the SW1 slide switch, because the OS102011 is only rated for 100 mA and cannot carry motor current itself. The switched rail VSW feeds the TB6612 VM (100 µF bulk + 100 nF) and the Nano VIN. The Nano's on-board 5 V regulator powers the TB6612 logic (VCC) and the QTR-8RC (~100 mA). Pins follow the brief exactly: QTR S1–S8 = D2, D4, D7, D8, D12, A0, A1, A2, LEDON = A3; PWMA D5, AIN1 D9, AIN2 D10, PWMB D6, BIN1 D11, BIN2 D3, STBY A4 (10 k pull-down so the motors stay off during reset/boot). The battery is read on A7 through a 10k/10k divider (ratio 2.0, 8.4 V → 4.2 V) with a 100 nF filter. CAL and GO share A6 through a resistor ladder: idle ≈5 V (ADC ~1023), GO ≈2.5 V (~512), CAL ≈0 V (~0). The status LED is on D13 with a 330 Ω resistor. Each motor has a 100 nF cap across its terminals. All grounds join at J1 pin 2 (star point).

powerBudget.notes: Average while running at ≤75% duty. Stall ~2.2 A at 8.4 V, so firmware must cap and ramp PWM.
ATmega328P + USB chip. The regulator drops (7.4 − 5) V × ~140 mA ≈ 0.34 W, which is fine.
About 29 min on 460 mAh at 80% usable (meets ≥ 20 min). Peaks of 3–4 A are possible on hard accelerations; F1 is a 3 A fast fuse, so the soft-ramp firmware is mandatory.

wiringSteps: SAFETY FIRST: unplug the LiPo from J1 and the USB cable from the Nano. Lift the robot so the wheels are off the table. Set SW1 to OFF (pin 3 side).

Solder the carrier PCB SMD parts first: F1, Q1, Q2 (check the SOT-23 orientation: G, S, D), R1–R8, C2, C3, C4, C7, C8. Then fit the through-hole parts: C1 (the + lead goes to VSW, the stripe goes to GND), SW1, SW2, SW3, D1 (long leg A goes to R7, flat side K goes to GND), J1, J3, J4 (JST S2B-PH-K-S), J2 (1x11 male), and the Nano and TB6612 female headers.
Check the ground net with a multimeter: J1 pin 2 must have continuity to both Nano GND header pins, all three TB6612 GND pins, J2 pin 2, the C1 '−' lead, SW1 pin 1, SW2 pin 3, R6, and D1 K.

Check the power path with a multimeter: J1 pin 1 → F1 → Q1 drain. Q1 source → Q2 source and R4. Q2 drain → TB6612 VM pin, C1 +, the Nano VIN header pin, and R1. Q1 gate → R3 → GND. Q2 gate → R4 and SW1 pin 2 (common).
Check that the Nano 5V header pin connects to the TB6612 VCC pin, J2 pin 1 and R5. Check there is NO continuity between 5V and VSW, or between either of them and GND.

Check the signal traces: Nano D5 → TB6612 PWMA, D9 → AIN1, D10 → AIN2, D6 → PWMB, D11 → BIN1, D3 → BIN2, A4 → STBY (with R8 10k to GND). Nano A7 → R1/R2 junction (C4 to GND). A6 → R5, SW2 pin 1, SW3 pin 1 and C7. SW3 pin 3 → R6 → GND. D13 → R7 → D1 A.
Check the QTR header traces: J2 pin 3 → D2, pin 4 → D4, pin 5 → D7, pin 6 → D8, pin 7 → D12, pin 8 → A0, pin 9 → A1, pin 10 → A2, pin 11 → A3.

Motors: solder a 100 nF cap across each motor's terminals (C5 on M1, C6 on M2). Solder the 26 AWG leads: red to the motor '+' (red-dot side), black to '−'. Crimp them into a PHR-2 housing: red in pin 1, black in pin 2. Feed the leads through the Ø6 plate holes. Plug the left motor M1 into J3 (pin 1 = A01, pin 2 = A02) and the right motor M2 into J4 (pin 1 = B01, pin 2 = B02).

QTR cable: solder the 1x11 header to the QTR-8RC. Make the 11-wire Dupont cable so each wire matches by LABEL. J2 pin 1 (VCC, red) → QTR VCC. J2 pin 2 (GND, black) → QTR GND. J2 pins 3–10 → QTR 1–8: yellow, green, blue, purple, grey, white, brown, orange. J2 pin 11 (pink) → QTR LEDON. Route it through the 20 x 4 mm plate slot.

Plug in the TB6612 breakout and the Nano (USB toward −X) without the battery. Connect USB. The Nano 5V should be about 4.7–5.0 V, D1 should respond to a blink sketch, and A7 should read about 0 (no battery). Upload a test that prints A6: ~1023 with no button, ~512 with GO pressed, ~0 with CAL pressed.

Battery: check the pack lead polarity with a meter. Red (+) must land on J1 pin 1 (BAT+) and black on pin 2. Disconnect USB, plug the LiPo into J1 with SW1 OFF, and confirm VSW (TB6612 VM) reads 0 V. Switch SW1 ON: VM should read the pack voltage (7.4–8.4 V) and Nano 5V should read 5.0 V.
Check A7: (ADC × 5/1023) × 2 should match the multimeter battery reading to within 0.1 V. Calibrate the scale factor in firmware if needed.

Motor test with the wheels lifted: STBY (A4) HIGH, 30% PWM on each channel in each direction. Note which IN1/IN2 combination drives each wheel forward and set the direction-invert constants in firmware. Then mount the PCB with M3x6 screws onto the 15 mm standoffs.
Final check: run QTR calibration (CAL), confirm all 8 channels read 0–1000 over the line, then do a low-speed run before raising speed. Never leave the LiPo connected unattended.
safetyNotes: LiPo: charge only off the robot with a balance charger at ≤ 1C (0.46 A). Never discharge below 3.3 V/cell (firmware cuts off at 6.6 V). Stop using the pack if it swells. Store at 3.8 V/cell in a LiPo bag.
Polarity: JST-PH is keyed, but re-terminated leads are often reversed. Check that red = J1 pin 1 before connecting. Q1 blocks a reversed pack but cannot fix a miswired harness elsewhere.
SW1 (OS102011, 100 mA rating) only switches the Q2 gate. Never rewire it to carry battery current directly.

The 6 V HP motors at 8.4 V can draw about 2.2 A at stall, above the TB6612's 1.2 A continuous rating. Firmware must cap PWM at 75% and soft-ramp it. Stop the motors if a wheel stalls for more than 0.5 s.
JST-PH connectors are rated about 2 A. Avoid long stalls, which can heat J1/J3/J4. F1 (3 A fast fuse) protects against shorts.
Keep the wheels off the surface or hold the robot during first power-up and while flashing. Any motor commands left over in a sketch will drive it off the table.
USB and battery can be connected together safely: the Nano's on-board diode separates USB 5 V from the VIN regulator. On USB alone, A7 reads 0 V and firmware must refuse to run the motors.
Do not short VSW to 5V. 8.4 V on the Nano 5V pin or the QTR VCC will destroy them.
Check the motor caps and bulk capacitor polarity (C1). A reversed electrolytic on VM can vent.

files.content:
[env:nano]
platform = atmelavr@5.0.0
board = nanoatmega328new
framework = arduino
monitor_speed = 115200
build_flags = -Os -Wall
lib_deps =
    pololu/QTRSensors@4.0.0

#pragma once
#include <Arduino.h>

// ---- QTR-8RC (J2) ----
static const uint8_t QTR_PINS[8] = {2, 4, 7, 8, 12, A0, A1, A2}; // nets QTR_S1..QTR_S8
#define PIN_QTR_LEDON A3      // QTR_LEDON
#define QTR_TIMEOUT_US 2500

// ---- TB6612FNG (U2) ----
#define PIN_PWMA 5            // MOTOR_A_PWM (left)
#define PIN_AIN1 9            // MOTOR_A_IN1
#define PIN_AIN2 10           // MOTOR_A_IN2
#define PIN_PWMB 6            // MOTOR_B_PWM (right)
#define PIN_BIN1 11           // MOTOR_B_IN1
#define PIN_BIN2 3            // MOTOR_B_IN2
#define PIN_STBY A4           // MOTOR_STBY (R8 pull-down)
// Flip if a wheel spins backwards on the bench test
#define LEFT_INVERT  false    // forward = AIN1 H / AIN2 L
#define RIGHT_INVERT true     // forward = BIN1 L / BIN2 H (mirrored motor)

// ---- UI ----
#define PIN_BUTTONS A6        // BUTTONS_A6 ladder: >768 none, 256-768 GO, <256 CAL
#define PIN_LED 13            // LED_DRIVE
#define BTN_NONE_TH 768
#define BTN_CAL_TH 256
#define BTN_DEBOUNCE_MS 40

// ---- Battery ----
#define PIN_VBAT A7           // VBAT_SENSE, divider 1:2
#define VBAT_SCALE (5.0f / 1023.0f * 2.0f)
#define VBAT_CUTOFF 6.6f
#define VBAT_RESUME 6.9f      // hysteresis before allowing a new run
#define VBAT_NOBATT 3.0f      // below this = USB only, motors locked out
#define VBAT_NOMINAL 7.4f     // PWM scaled to keep speed constant vs sag
#define VBAT_LOW_COUNT 50     // consecutive low samples (~0.5 s @10ms)

// ---- Motion ----
#define PWM_MAX 191           // 75% duty cap (TB6612 / 6V motor protection)
#define BASE_SPEED 150        // straight-line PWM @7.4V; raise for >1 m/s
#define RAMP_STEP 3           // max PWM change per loop (soft ramp)
#define CAL_SPEED 70
#define CAL_TIME_MS 2000
#define SEARCH_SPEED 110
#define LOST_DELAY_MS 300
#define LOST_STOP_MS 2000
#define LINE_THRESHOLD 200    // max calibrated value below = no line

// ---- PID (error in -3500..3500) ----
// Tune: raise KP until it oscillates, back off 30%, then add KD to damp.
#define KP 0.08f
#define KI 0.0f
#define KD 0.9f
#define I_LIMIT 20000.0f
#define LOOP_US 1000          // >=500 Hz target; QTR read dominates

build: Install VS Code + PlatformIO IDE (or `pip install platformio`)
Connect Nano USB (battery switch OFF is fine) and run: pio run -t upload
Bench test: wheels up, battery ON, CAL — check both wheels spin opposite in place; if a wheel spins wrong way flip LEFT_INVERT/RIGHT_INVERT
First-run: set robot across the line, press CAL (2 s spin), verify min/max dump shows clear contrast, place on line, press GO
Tune KP/KD then raise BASE_SPEED toward 1 m/s
notes: PWM capped at 191 (75%) and soft-ramped; PWM scaled by 7.4/Vbat to hold speed as the battery sags.
On USB-only power A7 reads ~0 V: motors locked out, calibration refused.
LED: solid = idle & calibrated, slow blink = uncalibrated, fast = calibrating, medium = running, short flash = low battery.
Line lost >300 ms -> pivot toward last-seen side; >2 s -> stop to IDLE.

assembly.title: Safety setup and parts check
assembly.description: Unplug the LiPo from J1 and the USB cable from the Nano. Set SW1 to OFF (pin 3 side). Lay out all parts by subsystem on an ESD mat and check them against the parts list.
assembly.caution: Keep the LiPo unplugged and away from the soldering area until step 15.

assembly.title: Solder carrier PCB SMD parts
assembly.description: Solder F1, Q1, Q2 (check SOT-23 pin order G, S, D), R1–R8, C2, C3, C4, C7 and C8. Solder the resistors, including the 330R LED resistor, the 10k divider top and the 10k divider bottom. Inspect the joints under magnification.
assembly.caution: Hot iron. Ventilate the area. Q1 and Q2 are ESD sensitive.

assembly.title: Solder through-hole parts on the PCB
assembly.description: Fit C1, the 100uF cap, with its + lead to VSW and its stripe to GND. Fit SW1, SW2 (the CAL button) and SW3 (the GO button). Fit D1, with the long leg A to R7 and the flat side K to GND. Fit J1, J3 and J4 (JST S2B-PH-K-S) and J2 (1x11 male). Fit the Nano and TB6612 female headers.
assembly.caution: Check the polarity of C1 and D1 before soldering.

assembly.title: Continuity checks: ground and power
assembly.description: Ground: J1 pin 2 must reach both Nano GND pins, all three TB6612 GND pins, J2 pin 2, the C1 − lead, SW1 pin 1, SW2 pin 3, R6 and D1 K. Power: J1 pin 1 → F1 → Q1 drain. Q1 source → Q2 source and R4. Q2 drain → TB6612 VM, C1 +, the Nano VIN pin and R1. Q1 gate → R3 → GND. Q2 gate → R4 and SW1 pin 2.

assembly.title: Continuity checks: 5V and signals
assembly.description: Nano 5V must connect to TB6612 VCC, J2 pin 1 and R5. There must be NO continuity between 5V and VSW, or from either to GND. Verify the signal traces: D5→PWMA, D9→AIN1, D10→AIN2, D6→PWMB, D11→BIN1, D3→BIN2, A4→STBY (R8 10k to GND), A7→R1/R2 junction, A6→R5/SW2/SW3/C7, D13→R7→D1. Verify J2 pins 3–11 → D2, D4, D7, D8, D12, A0, A1, A2, A3.
assembly.caution: Do not power the board until all shorts are ruled out.

assembly.title: Prepare the chassis plate and caster
assembly.description: Place the 3/4in steel ball in the caster housing with spacers. Fasten the housing under the front deck with the two M2.5x8 screws and M2.5 nuts. Tighten until snug and check that the ball rolls freely.
assembly.caution: Do not overtighten; the housing is plastic.

assembly.title: Prepare the motors
assembly.description: Solder a 100 nF cap across each motor's terminals (C5 on the left, C6 on the right). Solder 26 AWG leads: red to the + (red-dot side) and black to −. Crimp each pair into a PHR-2 housing, red in pin 1 and black in pin 2.
assembly.caution: Keep the soldering time short to protect the motor brushes.

assembly.title: Mount the motor brackets and motors
assembly.description: Clamp each motor into its bracket. Fasten each bracket to the underside of the chassis plate with two M2x8 screws (L rear, L front, R rear, R front). Feed the motor leads up through the Ø6 plate holes.
assembly.caution: Screws are short, so do not overtighten.

assembly.title: Fit the wheels
assembly.description: Press the D-shafts into the wheels so each wheel sits on its flat. Press the wheels onto the motor shafts, leaving a small gap from the bracket. Check that they spin freely.

assembly.title: Build the QTR cable and sensor
assembly.description: Solder the 1x11 header to the QTR-8RC. Build the 11-wire ribbon with Dupont housings by label: pin 1 red VCC, pin 2 black GND, pins 3–10 yellow, green, blue, purple, grey, white, brown, orange to QTR 1–8, pin 11 pink to LEDON. Check that the sensor row (QRE1113) is intact.
assembly.caution: Check the housing orientation against the labels before plugging in.

assembly.title: Mount the QTR array
assembly.description: Fit the M2x18 nylon standoffs to the front of the plate and secure the QTR board with the M2x5 nylon screws. Secure the standoffs to the plate with the M2x6 screws. Set the sensor height to 2.5 mm above the floor and route the ribbon through the 20 x 4 mm slot.
assembly.caution: Nylon threads strip easily, so use light torque.

assembly.title: Install the PCB standoffs
assembly.description: Fasten the four M3x15 standoffs (LR, RR, LF, RF) to the plate from underneath with the M3x6 bottom screws. Use a small drop of threadlocker on each. Torque to about 0.5 N·m.

assembly.title: Install the battery
assembly.description: Stick the EVA foam pad on the deck between the standoffs. Lay the LiPo on it with the leads toward the rear. Secure it with the hook-and-loop strap. Check the polarity of the red and black discharge leads with a meter, and confirm the JST PHR-2 plug has red on pin 1. Tuck the balance lead. Do not connect it yet.
assembly.caution: LiPo: do not puncture or short the leads. Keep the plug unconnected.

assembly.title: Bench test the PCB without battery
assembly.description: Plug the TB6612 breakout and the Nano (USB toward −X) into the PCB. Connect USB only. Check that Nano 5V reads 4.7–5.0 V, that D1 blinks with a test sketch, and that A7 reads about 0. Check that A6 reads about 1023 with no button, about 512 with GO, and about 0 with CAL.

assembly.title: Flash the firmware
assembly.description: Install VS Code and PlatformIO. Run `pio run` to fetch atmelavr 5.0.0 and QTRSensors 4.0.0. Connect the Nano USB and run `pio run -t upload`. Open `pio device monitor -b 115200`.

assembly.title: Mount the PCB and connect the wiring
assembly.description: Place the carrier PCB on the standoffs and fasten it with four M3x6 screws (RL, RR, FL, FR). Plug the left motor into J3 and the right into J4. Plug the Dupont cable into J2, with the QTR end matched to the labels.
assembly.caution: Do not pinch the leads between the PCB and the standoffs.

assembly.title: First power-up
assembly.description: With SW1 OFF, plug the LiPo into J1. Confirm that VM reads 0 V. Switch SW1 ON and confirm that VM reads 7.4–8.4 V and Nano 5V reads 5.0 V. Switch OFF immediately if there is heat, smell or a wrong reading.
assembly.caution: LiPo: stay with the robot, with the wheels lifted.

assembly.title: Calibrate battery measurement and motor direction
assembly.description: Check that (ADC × 5/1023) × 2 matches the meter to within 0.1 V, and adjust the scale in firmware if needed. With the wheels lifted, run 30% PWM in each direction. Set LEFT_INVERT and RIGHT_INVERT so both wheels spin forward. Reflash with `pio run -t upload` if needed.
assembly.caution: Keep the wheels off the table and your fingers clear.

assembly.title: Line calibration and functional test
assembly.description: Place the robot across the line and press CAL for the 2 s spin. Check that the min/max dump shows clear contrast and that all 8 channels read 0–1000 over the line. Place it on the line and press GO for a low-speed run. Tune KP/KD, then raise BASE_SPEED toward 1 m/s. Check the low-battery cutoff.
assembly.caution: Never leave the LiPo connected unattended.

review.summary: The architecture is sensible: Nano, TB6612 and QTR-8RC are a well-known line-follower combination, and the netlist and firmware pins are consistent. The design has several real problems. Motors are overvolted on a 6V rating and the mass target is missed. The envelope overshoots and the battery runtime claim is not supported by the numbers. A few electrical details also need rework: the reverse-polarity MOSFET gate, the Nano VIN path, and the button ladder.

checks.detail: All purchased parts have part numbers

checks.detail: 69 of 79 CAD parts linked to a BOM line

checks.name: Mass estimates agree
checks.detail: BOM mass 147 g vs CAD part mass 181 g

checks.name: Assembly covers the parts
checks.detail: 79 of 79 parts appear in 19 steps (100%)

checks.name: Motor voltage vs rating
checks.detail: 6V HP motors run directly from 7.4–8.4V (23–40% over rating). That gives the 1.6 m/s top speed but shortens brush and gearbox life. Stall current is about 1.6 A per motor against the TB6612's 1.2 A continuous rating. Cap PWM duty at about 75% (roughly 6.3V RMS).

checks.name: Runtime vs power budget
checks.detail: The budget lists 940 mA, while the automated check estimates 1877 mA. At 940 mA, 460 mAh gives about 29 min at 100% capacity. A 25C LiPo cut off at about 6.4V gives maybe 20 min at best. At 1.9 A it is under 12 min. The 20 min target is not demonstrated.

checks.name: Reverse-polarity P-MOSFET gate
checks.detail: Q1 uses AO3401A with Vgs max ±12V and a 10k gate resistor to GND. At 8.4V this is within limits, but the gate drive and body-diode orientation need confirming. Q2 gate is pulled to the switched rail via R4 and SW1 pulls it to GND, which is fine. Q2's Vgs of 8.4V is within limit. Add a gate zener or divider for margin.

checks.name: Nano VIN feed at 8.4V
checks.detail: The Nano's linear regulator is fed 8.4V and has to supply 5V to the QTR (100 mA) and the logic. Dissipation is about (8.4−5)×0.13 A ≈ 0.45 W, which is warm but tolerable. The VIN/VM rail also carries motor switching noise, so the 100 nF C3 decoupling is thin.

checks.name: Button ladder on A6
checks.detail: CAL is wired directly to A6 and GND (SW2.3). GO goes through R6 to give a 512 reading. The ladder is workable. A6 is analog-only on the Nano, so no internal pull-up is available. External R5 handles this, but the thresholds should have margin.

checks.name: Envelope and mass
checks.detail: CAD bounds are 108×81×94 mm against the 84×58 mm brief. BOM mass is 147 g and CAD mass is 181 g, against a ≤130 g target. Both mass figures exceed the target, and the 20% gap between BOM and CAD is unexplained.

checks.name: Sensor geometry and stability
checks.detail: The sensor is 68 mm ahead of the axle with a 47 mm wheelbase. The 74.9 mm array is wider than the 76 mm track width allows for clearance. Holding 2.5–3.0 mm of height depends on the 3/4in caster and the 3 mm plate, with no tolerance stack. The long lever arm makes 1 m/s tuning hard.

checks.name: Control loop rate
checks.detail: The QTR-RC read uses a 2500 µs timeout. White-surface reads finish sooner, but a loop with a line on black takes about 2.5 ms, so 400 Hz is realistic. The ≥500 Hz target is optimistic. A blocking read also delays battery and button handling.

checks.name: Line-lost and state logic
checks.detail: Lost-line handling has a brief hold on the last turn, then a pivot search, then a stop. The low-battery state uses a debounce count with hysteresis (VBAT_RESUME). Motors are disabled in IDLE and LOWBATT. This is sound.

checks.name: PID derivative and speed scaling
checks.detail: The derivative term has no dt normalisation or filtering. The integral accumulates per iteration with a clamp. Base speed is halved when |err|>2500, a crude step that can cause jerk at 1 m/s.

checks.name: Cost and availability
checks.detail: The BOM totals $144.80 including a $12 chassis plate and a $24.90 genuine Nano. The listed lines sum to less than the total. Part numbers are real and standard. A Turnigy 460 mAh cell is a cheap hobby part with variable availability.

checks.name: Assembly order
checks.detail: The PCB-standoff and QTR steps come after the wheels are fitted. The battery is installed under the PCB on 15 mm standoffs, with 15 mm of clearance. The battery is hard to service without unscrewing the PCB. The SMD parts listed in the netlist (0603) conflict with the through-hole BOM resistors (1/4W).

checks.name: BOM vs netlist parts
checks.detail: The netlist lists a 3A fuse, two AO3401A MOSFETs, 100k R4, 10µF C8 and a 100 µF EEE-FK electrolytic. The BOM has none of the fuse, MOSFETs, 100k or 10µF parts. The BOM's 0.1 µF ceramics and 1/4W resistors differ from the 0805/0603 SMD parts in the netlist.

checks.name: LiPo handling
checks.detail: A 3A fast fuse, reverse-polarity protection, firmware low-voltage cutoff at the 2S level and a power switch are all present. The battery is held with a velcro strap and foam pad. A 3A fuse is fine for a 1.9A peak load, though the LiPo should still be charged in a bag.

suggestions: Reconcile the BOM with the netlist: add the fuse, the two AO3401A parts, R4 100k and C8 10µF. Specify SMD resistor and capacitor packages to match the PCB.
Rework the power budget (940 mA vs 1877 mA). Recompute runtime against real motor load and the usable LiPo capacity, or move to a larger cell.
Reduce mass to ≤130 g (a lighter plate or PCB) and tighten the envelope, or update the brief to match the 108×81 mm CAD.
Limit the PWM duty cap, or use 10:1/6V-appropriate motors, to protect the 6V motors and keep stall current under the TB6612 rating.
Add a stronger VIN filter, such as a 10 µF cap or a ferrite bead, and consider a dedicated 5V buck for the sensor.
Make the QTR read non-blocking, or use a shorter timeout (about 1500 µs), and add dt-normalised, filtered D.
Add a tolerance stack and height-adjustment shims for the 2.5–3.0 mm sensor height.
Change the assembly order so the battery can be swapped without removing the PCB.
